windows.note: tools/gearing.js: each mesh's depthing window about its drawn centres (mm), the hole position tolerance (mm) aimed at the drawn centres, and its mean pressure angle (deg, frictionless contact); read by thermal.js and fea.py

bench.title: The mainspring's torque
bench.when: before it goes into the barrel, and again in the barrel
bench.how: Hold the barrel and turn its arbor with a lever and weights or a torque gauge: a 3D-printed lever 50 mm long and a hanging weight do (1 kg at 50 mm is 0.49 N·m). Wind it up from let down by its set-up and read the torque each half turn over the 4.51 turns the fusee uses, then unwind and read again (the spring's friction is the difference). Leave it wound a week and read again. Once, in its barrel, wind it on from let down until its coils lie tight on the arbor and count the turns: from its slack to there it must have the set-up and the fusee's 4.61 turns with half a turn to spare (the model's spring has 0.60: so near coil-bound the coils' friction takes up to 5 % of its pull running, mainspring_friction.py, and the swing falls under the manual's for the first hours after each wind).
bench.pass: Fully wound 0.74-0.86 N·m (the model's 0.78; the band keeps the balance in the manual's 1⅜-1½ turns: tools/tolerances.js); falling about 84 mN·m a turn, to about 0.40 N·m when the fusee's chain is all on the barrel. After the week, still inside the band (a spring that sets more is replaced, or set up a tooth: Op. 13). Unwinding it reads less than winding: the coils' friction gives 3-6 % on the model's spring, mainsprings run 10-20 % under their winding (ICMFF9: 11-22 % read so; the strip's edges and its steel too); over 22 %, clean and grease it.

bench.title: The fusee evens the pull
bench.when: the chain on, the barrel set up, before the train goes in
bench.how: With the fusee wheel's arbor on a torque gauge (or the same lever on its square), read the torque each half turn of the fusee, from fully wound (the chain on the fusee's top turn) to run down, 17.5 half turns.
bench.pass: Every reading within -5 to +11 % of their mean (the model's even 311 mN·m): the escape wheel's torque in that band swings the balance 247.5-270° (the escapement's ampAt). A reading outside it at one end means the fusee's profile and the spring's stiffness don't match: the set-up moves the whole curve, not its slope.

bench.title: The train's depths
bench.when: the plates and bridges bored, before the jewels and bushes go in
bench.how: Measure each pair of holes' centres with gauge pins in them and a micrometer (or on a measuring machine), on the plate and on the bridge. Then the arbors in, each mesh tried in turn, the escape wheel held: feel the shake at the pinion and watch the teeth through a loupe as the wheel is turned slowly.
bench.pass: Centres 20.383, 16.550, 11.297, 10.444 mm (fusee-centre, centre-third, third-fourth, fourth-escape), each within ±13 µm (tools/gearing.js: the wheel's tips stay off the pinion's root with the pivots' shake taken off). Every mesh turns smoothly with shake at its pinion; none butts or catches. A hole that errs should err wide: each mesh takes several times as much wide as close. One closer than its window's close side less the pivots' shake (48, 39, 28, 27 µm close): re-bush the hole, the bush bored on the drawn centre (benchcheck.py).

bench.title: Endshake
bench.when: each arbor in its bearings, before the escapement goes in
bench.how: Lift each arbor by its wheel with tweezers and watch the shoulder against a dial indicator, or feel it.
bench.pass: 28-73 µm at 20 °C (Ops. 15, 69 and 74's 0.001-0.003 in, less what the brass takes from it at 40 °F and gives at 100 °F: tools/thermal.js).

bench.title: The balance and its hairspring vibrated
bench.when: the hairspring pinned to its collet and stud, the balance on its staff
bench.how: Vibrate the balance with its spring in a vibrating tool (or the cock on a holder) against a master or a phone's timer: count the oscillations over two minutes, or record the beat (python acoustic.py FILE reads a recording).
bench.pass: 2 oscillations a second (7,200 an hour): Table II's balance (578.5 g·mm²) wants a spring of 91.4 µN·m a radian. Within 40 s a day of it (one turn of the timing weights, Sec. IX) before the spring goes in; the weights take up the rest.

bench.title: The detent rings
bench.when: the detent made, before it goes in
bench.how: Clamp its foot as the block holds it (a printed jig with the foot's two screws does), the stone and the blade's end free of everything, and flick the end of the blade lightly with a hair or a pith stick. Record the ring with a phone held a few millimetres off and read its lowest strong pitch with a spectrum app, or python benchcheck.py --ring FILE (any recording ffmpeg reads). The trip spring rings too, near 738 Hz: the detent's own is the lower.
bench.pass: 137 Hz with the spring as drawn (0.079 mm thick); 137-342 Hz for a spring 0.079-0.150 mm thick. The pitch goes nearly as the thickness to the 1.5: it measures the spring's section, which no source gives. Lower, the spring is thinner than drawn and the detent rings more after each lock (a held tooth's stone lifted up to 56 % of the depth of lock, against 23 % as drawn: tools/tripping.js); higher than 342 Hz, unlocking takes too much of the impulse (tools/tolerances.js). From about 194 Hz (0.10 mm) it rings least (the stone 16 % of the depth of lock).

bench.title: The escapement's figures
bench.when: the detent, its springs and the balance in; the train's power let down to the set-up
bench.how: Turn the balance slowly by hand with a protractor on the cock (a printed card under the balance does) and read each angle where the manual's operations read it, through a loupe; the roller's shake and the horn's clearance with feeler gauges.
bench.pass: The manual's figures: lock about 6° (the model 5.5°, Op. 85), let-off at least 6° (8.7°, Op. 86), overall 26-30° (28.0°, Op. 87), drop about 2° (2.0°, Op. 97), the horn's clearance to the unlocking jewel about 0.010 in (0.25 mm, Op. 88), roller shake about 0.002 in (0.056 mm, Op. 84). Set them with the lock-adjusting and detent-adjusting screws and the trip spring's tip (Ops. 84-97); the detent spring's preload by Op. 78's weight, 0.770 g on the locking jewel. Never a lock under 5°: shallower, the detent's ringing after each lock comes to over half the depth of lock (102 µm at the stone at 5°), the drop is gone at 3.4° and a tooth gets past at 2.4° (tools/tripping.js). Against knocks it is the preload that holds, not the lock: the blow that trips it changes little with the lock (53-61 g over 3 ms).

bench.title: The swing
bench.when: the movement running, fully wound and again run down
bench.how: Read the balance's swing by eye against marks on the cock, from a phone's slow-motion video (the screws' sweep), or from a recording of the beat (python acoustic.py FILE fits the escapement's clicks to the model in time).
bench.pass: 1⅜-1½ turns, 247.5-270° each way, fully wound and run down alike (Sec. II, Sec. IX). Low at both ends: the train's freedom or the depths; low at one end only: the fusee and the spring (the fusee test); high: the mainspring is too strong for its band.

bench.title: The winding stop takes a strong hand
bench.when: the stop-bar and the winding stop made, then wound to the stop
bench.how: Harden and temper the stop-bar and the stud (a file skates on them). Wind to full wind and hold the key against the stop with a torque gauge (or a lever and a weight) up to 1.06 N·m, a strong hand's on the key's paddle (overwind.js).
bench.pass: Nothing moves or marks: hardened, the stop-bar's end yields at 2.72 N·m and the stud's thread at 3.86; left soft the bar bends at 1.01, a strong hand's. The first thing to give is the key's own socket (1.60 N·m). Never turn the key the wrong way: 0.19 N·m clockwise bends the fusee wheel's teeth (the build's key has a ratchet in its pipe).

bench.title: The pawls' springs
bench.when: the maintaining work assembled, before the fusee wheel goes on
bench.how: Lift each winding pawl out of its tooth with a pegwood and let it go: it must snap back. Measure each spring's set: lift its end off the pawl's arm and read how far it stands past the arm when free, with a feeler or under a loupe against a scale. The sustaining pawl's wire stands in its hole with the pawl turned in about 0.12 rad (7°) from where its tip meets the ratchet.
bench.pass: Each winding pawl's spring set at least 0.08 mm (twice that is the aim): less, and when the key lets go the fusee's teeth can outrun the pawl and catch it part way in (ratchets.js): bend it back to the aim. The sustaining pawl's wire must press the pawl into the teeth (0.12 rad is the aim): from any wire that does, the pawl falls from a tip to the root in 4.9 ms or less, inside the 8.3 ms a tooth takes at a turn a second of the key (ratchets.js); one that leaves the pawl loose in its tooth, bend it in. The pawls drawn in by their load: the winding pawls' faces bear square (a draw of 12.5°), the sustaining pawl's end stoned to bear along its tooth's face, not on its corner.

bench.title: The maintaining work drives the train
bench.how: Turn the key back a little (winding) and hold it still, the fusee off the train: watch the balance and time how long it keeps swinging.
bench.pass: Five to ten minutes (Sec. IV), the swing falling slowly; a winding never takes so long. Under a minute, the sustaining spring is too soft or closes solid under the drive: its section and gap are estimates (OPEN-QUESTIONS.md, sustaining.js).

bench.title: The cannon pinion's friction
bench.when: the motion work and the hands on, the movement level
bench.how: Hang a weight on the minute hand 40 mm from its arbor, the hand horizontal, and see whether it turns the hand (the cannon pinion slipping on the centre arbor; Op. 58).
bench.pass: It slips between 3.5 and 93 g (motionwork.js: tighter, setting the hands forward drives the escapement to trip; looser, a knock turns the hands): set it near 18 g.

bench.title: The rate, and the Navy's test
bench.when: the movement in its box, cased and in its gimbals
bench.how: Each day at the same hour compare it with a time signal (radio, GPS, or a network time service read on a phone) to the tenth of a second, and keep the log: python rating.py LOG.csv works the daily rates, the Navy test's figures and what it would carry at sea. For temperature, keep it a week each at about 55, 72½ and 90 °F (a wine cooler, a room, a box with a lamp and a thermostat), as the Navy test does.
bench.pass: Good enough to navigate by: its daily rate steady, whatever it is, the navigator carrying it. The Navy's test (Sec. IX, the working model's thirty-day test card) is the yardstick: regulation, the largest mean daily rate of any period, within 1.55 s a day; rating, the mean deviation of the daily rates, 0.50; the largest difference between two daily rates in a period 0.75; the mean rates at 90 and 72½, 72½ and 55, and 90 and 55 °F within 0.75, 0.75 and 1.20; recovery 0.70; isochronism, the 12-hour rate against half the 24-hour, 0.50. Then rating.py's voyage: what it would carry after 30 days, 4 s of time a mile of longitude on the equator. Out on the 90 against 55 °F figure, move balance screw pairs along the rim by Table IV (Op. 8; each keeps its head, so the rate stands): a pair moved toward the quarter (hole 7) loses in heat, toward the arm's ends gains; from the standard set the moves reach -6.5 to +4.6 s a day, in steps of 0.42 s or less (tools/deviations.js). Past that the spring's coefficient is further off than they take up: its hardening moves it, or another spring is fitted.

devs.title: Mainspring in Nivaflex 45/5
devs.period: Straumann's Nivaflex: patented 1948, the name registered 1957
devs.vmat: Nivaflex 45/5 (Co 45, Ni 21, Cr 18, Fe 5, W 4, Mo 4, Ti 1, Be 0.2 %)
devs.vtreat: cold-drawn strip 0.386 mm thick (0.379-0.400 keeps the manual's swing) × 13.55 mm × 1064 mm, aged 2 h at 500 °C to over 3000 N/mm²; coiled; greased
devs.why: The same torque from a strip 0.386 mm thick (E 220 GPa against carbon steel's 207), so the fusee, the swing and the rate are unchanged. Fully wound it is stressed 2309 MPa, a margin of 1.30 on Nivaflex's 3000 N/mm² against carbon steel's 1.13-1.17; it doesn't take a set, rust in salt air or magnetize, so its pull, and with it the rate, holds steady over the months a navigator carries it.
sources: Jacques Allemann, Nivaflex 45/5 data sheet JAS-014 (2021): composition, E 220 GPa, density 8.50, expansion 11.2 × 10⁻⁶/K, strength over 3000 N/mm², non-magnetic, corrosion
Vacuumschmelze, Nivaflex 45/18 brochure: tensile strength up to 2900 MPa, hardness up to 800 HV, mainsprings among its uses
Nivaflex, Wikipedia; R. Straumann, Grail-Watch wiki: patented 1948, Nivaflex SA, the name registered 1957

devs.title: Hairspring in Nivarox, the balance the Model 21's
devs.period: Nivarox (Straumann, perfected 1933, patented 1935), offered graded to a balance by 1940
devs.vmat: Nivarox (Fe-Ni-Cr-Be, self-compensating), graded for a monometallic balance
devs.vtreat: the same helix and terminal curves (hairspring.js), the strip 0.215-0.228 mm × 0.23 mm; its thermoelastic coefficient about +7 × 10⁻⁶ a °C (0 to 13 for the Model 21's balance; Table IV takes up -5.5 to +7.7 of it); vibrated to the balance, its length taken at the stud
devs.why: Elinvar springs heat-treated to suit a balance can't be bought; Nivarox, graded to a balance's expansion, can. The Model 21's own balance is kept: its stainless rim on an Invar arm expands as a 15-17 × 10⁻⁶ a °C metal would (Table IV's figures, read as the rim's bending, give it), so the spring wants 0 to 13 × 10⁻⁶ a °C, about what Nivarox is graded to for bronze balances. What the spring misses, Table IV's screw moves (Op. 8) trim on the bench: -6.5 to +4.6 s a day between 55 and 90 °F, in steps of 0.42 s or less, so a spring -5.5 to +7.7 × 10⁻⁶ a °C off its mark still meets the Navy's 1.20. A one-piece Glucydur balance (the build's until 13 October 2026) has nothing to trim and would need the spring held to ±1.4, a seventh of what a bought spring holds. Nivarox's expansion and modulus are estimated: the temperature test (the bench's last) settles it.
sources: Nivarox, Wikipedia; WatchesbySJX, "Hairspring Materials and Evolution Part II" (2025); VintageWatchstraps, "Nivarox balance springs": Fe-Ni-Cr-Be, its thermoelastic coefficient set by alloy and heat treatment, graded for monometallic balances; perfected 1933, patented 1935
EP3502288A1 (Nivarox-FAR): an alloy's thermoelastic coefficient within ±10 ppm/°C gives an oscillator within ±0.6 s a day a °C
The manual: Sec. II (the stainless rim, Invar arm and Elinvar spring), Table IV (p. 74) and Op. 8
S. Timoshenko, Strength of Materials, Part II: a thin ring's bending by Fourier series; Roark's Formulas for Stress and Strain: a ring under two opposite forces

devs.title: Winding key with a one-way ratchet
devs.period: Breguet's "tipsy" key, about 1790: a ratchet in the key's pipe
devs.vmat: brass, as the Model 21's key, with a steel ratchet wheel on the socket and a click in the pipe, sprung
devs.vtreat: the socket turns the fusee counterclockwise (seen from the key) and slips the other way; the Model 21's plain key kept to set the hands
devs.why: Turned the wrong way, the plain key's torque goes through the winding pawls and the sustaining spring into the train, which the escapement holds still: 0.19 N·m bends the fusee wheel's teeth (overwind.js), about a third of what an average hand gives the key's paddle (0.63 N·m, Imrhan and Munoz-Vasa 2013). The manual's "counterclockwise" is all that prevents it. A ratchet in the key's pipe slips the wrong way, so it can't happen; wound the right way the stop takes a strong hand with 1.5 times to spare. The hands still set with the plain key: they go forward clockwise on the dial's side, which a winding-only key would turn back.
sources: S. N. Imrhan and M. J. Munoz-Vasa, "Finger Pinch Loosening and Tightening Torques on Small Cylindrical Handles Among Industrial Workers", Industrial and Systems Engineering Review 1(2), 2013 (and Swain et al. 1970 there)
The manual: Sec. III and IV (the key wound counterclockwise, the hands set forward), Tool 47
Breguet's "tipsy" key (clé de sûreté), about 1790: a ratchet in the key that slips when turned the wrong way
